'''Izumi Inoue Shrine''' ({{lang|ja|泉井上神社}}, ''Izumi Inoue Jinja'') is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine}} located in {{ill|Izumi, Osaka|ar|إزومي (أوساكا)|ca|Izumi (Osaka)|ce|Идзуми (Осака)|ceb|Izumi Shi (distrito sa Hapon, Ōsaka-fu)|cs|Izumi (Ósaka)|cy|Izumi, Osaka|de|Izumi (Osaka)|eo|Izumi (Osaka)|es|Izumi (Osaka)|et|Izumi|fa|ایزومی، اوساکا|fi|Izumi (Osaka)|fr|Izumi (Osaka)|gl|Izumi, Ōsaka|hy|Իզումի|it|Izumi (Osaka)|ja|和泉市|ko|이즈미시 (오사카부)|mzn|ایزومی، اوساکا|nl|Izumi (Osaka)|no|Izumi|pl|Izumi (Osaka)|pt|Izumi (Osaka)|ro|Izumi, Osaka|ru|Идзуми (Осака)|sh|Izumi|sr|Изуми|sv|Izumi, Ōsaka|tg|Изуми|th|อิซูมิ (จังหวัดโอซากะ)|tl|Izumi, Osaka|tr|Izumi, Osaka|tt|Идзуми (Осака)|uk|Ідзумі (Осака)|ur|ایزومی، اوساکا|vi|Izumi, Ōsaka|war|Izumi, Osaka|zh|和泉市|zh_classical|和泉市|zh_min_nan|Izumi-chhī|zh_yue|和泉|qid=Q696412}}, Japan. It is an ancient shrine listed in the {{ill|Engishiki|en|Engishiki}} and was historically the {{ill|Sōja|en|Sōja}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Izumi Province|en|Izumi Province}}. The shrine also hosts the Izumi Gosha Sōja within its precincts, enshrining the five main shrines of Izumi.

== History ==
The precise date of establishment is unknown. According to legend, the shrine originated when Empress Jingū visited the area during the 2nd year of Emperor Chūai’s reign. A miraculous spring is said to have appeared, which became a sacred site, and a shrine was built to enshrine the spring as a divine blessing.

The spring, known as "Izumi Shimizu" (Izumi Clear Water), is considered the namesake of Izumi Province and Izumi City.<ref name="asahi">Asahi Newspaper, Osaka Edition, November 12, 2013, p. 32.</ref>

When Izumi Province was formally established in 716 CE, the shrine became the center of the provincial capital. The Izumi Gosha Sōja was later built within the precincts, enshrining deities from the province's most prominent shrines.<ref name="asahi"/>

During the medieval period, the distinction between Izumi Inoue Shrine and the Izumi Gosha Sōja diminished. Under the influence of {{ill|Hachiman faith|en|Hachiman faith}}, the shrine became known as I-no-Hachiman-gū. Prominent warlords, including {{ill|Kusunoki Masashige|en|Kusunoki Masashige}} and {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|en|Toyotomi Hideyoshi}}, revered the shrine.

In the Edo period, the shrine’s lands and holdings were significantly reduced. It regained prominence in the Meiji era, and in 1908, Izumi Inoue Shrine was re-established as the primary shrine, with the Izumi Gosha Sōja as a subsidiary shrine.

== Features ==
; main hall
The main hall was reconstructed in 1895 and is built in the {{ill|Taisha-zukuri|en|Taisha-zukuri|qid=Q387874|lt=Ōtori-zukuri}} architectural style. It houses the primary deity, the Three Divine Creators.

; Izumi Shimizu
This sacred spring, historically significant for the region, is designated as an Osaka Prefecture historic site. Although it no longer flows, it was once a vital water source for the area.

== Events ==
; Autumn Grand festival
The festival takes place in October and features traditional rituals, including a ''danjiri'' (float) procession. Historical records indicate the festival dates back to 1585.

== Cultural Properties ==
=== National Important Cultural Properties ===
* '''Izumi Gosha Sōja main hall''' - Designated in 1924.<ref>{{National Cultural Property Database|102|2201}}</ref>

=== Osaka Prefecture Cultural Properties ===
* '''Izumi Inoue Shrine Stone Tablet Pagoda''' - A relic of the Nanboku-chō period, designated in 1970.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Osaka Prefecture Designated Cultural Properties|url=http://www.pref.osaka.lg.jp/bunkazaihogo/bunkazai/kenzou.html}}</ref>

=== Osaka Prefecture Historic Sites ===
* '''Izumi Shimizu''' - Designated in 1971.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Osaka Prefecture Historic Sites|url=http://www.pref.osaka.lg.jp/bunkazaihogo/bunkazai/kenzou.html}}</ref>
